title: Who is hearing?
hookLine: Bassui: ask who is it that hears?

cards: Right now there's a sound near you. A fridge humming. Traffic.
A bird. A moment ago you didn't notice it; now you do. Put a strange question next to that sound.
Not what is it, but who is it that's hearing it? It sounds like a riddle for a sleepy afternoon.
A Japanese Zen teacher named Bassui made it central to his teaching, and told students to keep asking until the question itself broke open.

teach.b: Bassui was a Rinzai Zen teacher in Japan who wrote letters and talks for monks, nuns and lay people, and again and again he gave them one question: when you hear a sound, who is hearing? First, why hearing?

teach.h: WHY HEARING? SOUND IS ALWAYS HERE.
teach.b: Sound is always arriving, so the question is always there. No temple or cushion needed, just ears. Second, what the question is not.
Bassui doesn't want an answer like my ears, or my brain, or me. Those are labels. He tells students to turn the attention back from the sound toward the one who hears, and look.

teach.h: LOOK FOR THE HEARER. FIND NO SHAPE.
teach.b: They find no object to grab: no shape, no color, nothing to point at. And yet the hearing is plainly happening. Third, the push.
When you can't find the hearer, don't give up and don't settle for a clever explanation.

teach.h: KEEP ASKING, WITH YOUR WHOLE BODY.
teach.b: Keep asking, more deeply, with your whole body, the way you'd keep searching for something precious you'd lost. He describes the questioning growing until it fills everything, and then, at last, breaking open.
Fourth, what it opens onto: your own mind, which he calls the true master, the Buddha nature that was never born and never dies.
It isn't far away or reserved for monks, Bassui insists. It's the one listening to this sentence. Zen teachers use questions in different ways; some give a koan, some ask students simply to sit.
Bassui's way was this one plain question, carried everywhere.

how: In some Rinzai Zen communities, teachers give students a single question such as Bassui's to carry through sitting and daily work, and check their understanding in private meetings.

games.q: you've asked who is hearing, looked, and found nothing at all. you're Bassui's student. what now?
o: decide the question is a trick and stop
games.why: Bassui says not to settle: keep asking with your whole body until the question breaks open.

practice: Sit still and let sounds come to you, near, far, loud, soft, without naming them. Then gently ask inside, who is hearing this, and instead of answering with a word, turn the attention back toward wherever the hearing is happening.
If you find nothing to hold, stay with the not-finding, and when the mind drifts, let the next sound call you back.

wordCard.voice: Bassui. The Zen teacher who told students, when a sound comes, to turn from it and ask who is hearing, and keep looking. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: stay with the not-finding. Every sound can bring the question back. See you tomorrow.
